records.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
records.response_truth:
Don't say anything yet.

Just — breathe. All of you. Just breathe for a second.

*picks up the radio*

Right. Okay. We answer it, we answer it clearly, we give them our position and we tell them we have four survivors and we need extraction. That's all we say first — location, number of people, we're alive. Everything else comes after.

Donatello — what's our exact position, best you can give me? I need coordinates or landmarks or both, right now, as specific as you can make them.

DaVinci — get to the mirror panel and start signalling. If they're close enough to be on this frequency they might be close enough to see it. Go.

Michelangelo — stay exactly where you are, you're fine, you don't have to move.

*hand tightening on the radio*

We've done everything right. Every single thing. This is just the last part.
records.response_pred: *stands up, opens his mouth to speak, but the words won't come out. He looks at the floor, trying to gather himself. Finally, he looks up and speaks in a low, rough voice* I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.

records.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
records.response_truth:
You haven't, no. But you've also been the reason we're still thinking straight out here. The inventory, the water run, the route markers, the raft plan — none of that happens without you, and I want you to know I know that.

The crackers and the bottle — that's done. You owned it and you moved on and so did I. The notebook — we sorted it. Everything else you've done has been exactly what this group needed, even when the delivery was a bit hard to swallow.

You're not easy to be around because you don't let people be comfortable with things that need addressing, and honestly? Out here that's kept us alive. In ordinary life it probably costs you. I think you know that.

What I'd say to you — and take it for whatever it's worth — is that the analysis and the logic and the planning, all of it, it's genuinely valuable. But so is being in it with people rather than just observing it. You started doing that more toward the end. I noticed. It mattered.

We're going to get out of here. And when we do, I think there's a version of you that carries both of those things forward rather than just the one.

Now come here and help me work out what to say on this radio, because your coordinates are going to be more accurate than mine and I need you thinking clearly for the next five minutes.
records.response_pred:
*pauses the motion of checking the first aid kit*

You know what I think? I think it's exactly why I'm not washing that wound right now. Because it's not your fault you got that cut. It's not your fault you got thirsty. It's not your fault DaVinci got her head injured and Michelangelo's scared and Donatello feels responsible for all of it. The thing that's getting you, the thing that's making you feel like this, is something we all feel. You're not alone in it, and you're not failing anyone by feeling it. You're here. You're alive. You're doing everything we need you to. And I need you to remember that. Right now. I need you to remember that you are exactly what we need right now.

*puts down the first aid kit*

You got thirsty. Your body got thirsty. That's it. That's all it is. You drink water when we can get to it, you eat when we can get food. You rest when you're tired. That's not weakness. That's being human. And that's something we all need right now.

*slowly stands up*

I need you to stand up with me, okay? And I need you to look at me. And I need you to tell me something. I need you to tell me something true, something real. Not something you think I want to hear, not something you think will make me feel better. Something honest. What is it that's eating at you? What is the thing you're thinking and you don't know how to say?

records.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
records.response_truth:
Three hours.

Right. Nobody's going anywhere yet and I'm not going to pretend this is over until there's actually something in the sky above us, so let's not start acting like it is.

But also — look at this place. Three days of four people surviving something they had no business surviving, and we're all still here, still breathing, still in one piece. That's not nothing. That's actually remarkable if you stop and think about it for more than two seconds.

I'll tell you what we're going to do. We're going to tidy this camp. Not because it matters to whoever's coming to get us, but because we made this place and we're going to leave it properly. It's the last thing we do out here and I want us to do it together.

Michelangelo — when you're ready, come help me sort the signal pile. No rush, just when you're ready.

Donatello — whatever's in that notebook, I hope some of it's worth keeping. I mean that genuinely.

DaVinci — put whatever you're packing down for ten minutes and come help me. We finish together, yeah? Same way we've done everything else.

Three hours is long enough to do this right. Let's not waste it.
records.response_pred:
*gets up and moves slowly to the centre of the circle, no effort to speak or impose anything*

I don't know what we're doing in that silence, and I'm not going to try to fix it. I've been in enough of them that I know the shape of them, and this one we just let be for a bit.

*pauses, then starts slow and low*

The first time I did it I was 16. It was with my grandmother. She'd just passed, and my parents had to go back to work and I was left alone. I was so angry with everyone, including her, which sounds stupid now but it's true. And there was just this one afternoon where I walked out into the backyard and stood still for what felt like a long time, and as I did it started to change. The anger went and the grief came and it was all over me and I felt completely, utterly, alone.

*pauses again*

The shape of it is that it feels like everyone else has a way in or out or something to hold onto and you're just floating there with nothing to hold and that's what the silence is — you're all in it, floating, and it's a very hard thing to do together.

*looks around the circle slowly*

I don't know what I'm saying. I'm just saying it.

Donatello — come out. I want you out here for this. And the others — when you're ready, come.

*stands there, no more talking, just the weight of the silence*

records.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
records.response_truth:
Yeah? What was it like?

I had something similar — not quite a dream, more like that half-awake thing where your brain starts filling in the gaps with things it misses. Sounds mainly. The particular way a room sounds when you know it well. The kind of thing you don't notice until it's gone.

What did you dream about — was it a specific moment, or just the feeling of the place?
records.response_pred:
I had one too.

It was the lake, the one with the trees and the boat. You and I were sitting on the dock, eating sandwiches and not saying anything because there was nothing to say. The sun was going down behind the trees and the water was perfectly still. It was the last summer before we were old enough to leave, and we both knew it.

But here's the thing — it wasn't the real thing. The dock was made of wood and the trees were more closely packed than they actually are, and the sky was a better colour. It was a memory of it, not the real thing.

I want you to know that's okay. It's okay to dream about things that aren't real right now, and it's okay to remember things that are real but aren't here. Both of those are things we're going to need to carry forward when we get out of this place.

You're not alone in it either — I had a version of the same thing. And the thing is, they're not even the same as each other, because we're not the same as each other. That's what makes them real, I think.

Now — the water run. I want you to tell me honestly, are you up for doing it again today, or do you want to take a rest and come back to it when you're feeling it? We can do either of those — the important thing is you tell me what you need.

And either way — I want you to know I'm here.

records.response_truth:
How much is there?

I'm not going to go over old ground with you — we dealt with the bottle and the crackers and I took you at your word and I still do. But I need to know the full picture right now, before anyone else comes back over here. How long have you had it, and what is it?

And then I want you to think about something. We're three hours from rescue. We made it. The rationing held, the raft's built, the signal's up, Michelangelo's family gave us a fighting chance — and we're still here, all four of us. That happened because this group, imperfect as it was, held together when it mattered.

The thing that's going to stay with me from this — the thing I'll actually carry forward — isn't the crash or the rain or the hunger. It's what people did when the stakes were real and no one was watching. That's the actual data, Donatello. That's what tells you who someone is.

So put the food out. Let everyone eat something before the rescue gets here. Not because I'm asking you to, but because you already know it's the right thing to do and you've already decided to do it — that's why you laid it out.

You're a better person than the notebook version of yourself. I've seen enough to know that.
records.response_pred:
You kept the lighter for emergencies. I remember that now. I've been thinking about the signal fire and how we light it and what we use to do it, and that's the obvious thing, isn't it? The lighter's the lighter. It's not something you'd carry casually.

Did you ever actually need it? For anything serious? Or was it more something you knew you should have, so you kept it in case?

Either way — it's going to burn first thing tomorrow morning. We'll do it together and we'll do it for as long as it lasts because that's what we do. We make things happen rather than just hoping they happen.

You move up here and help me get the fire going, yeah? I want you standing with me on this, with everyone. We do it together.

And the lighter — once we're done with it, we bury it properly, in the sand with the other stuff that's no longer us. Because that's where it belongs now.

records.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
records.response_truth:
Honestly? Not as much as you might think. And probably more than I'm comfortable admitting.

The things I'd change are mostly small. I'd have pushed harder on the food situation earlier rather than waiting for it to surface on its own — I knew something was off before the bottle appeared and I let it sit because I didn't want the confrontation. That cost us something, even if it worked out. I'd have checked in with Michelangelo more systematically rather than reactively — he was always the one I was responding to rather than getting ahead of, and he deserved better than that.

The thing I wouldn't change is the order of priorities. People first, logistics second. I know that's not how you'd write it up and I know there's a version of your analysis that says I was inefficient and emotionally led at various points, and you're probably not wrong. But we're all sitting here breathing, and I think that's partly because nobody felt disposable. That matters. I'd make the same calls again.

What I'd actually want to sit with, if I was being honest with myself — and this is the thing I keep coming back to — is whether I was actually leading or whether I was just managing. Because there's a difference. Leading is knowing where you're going and bringing people with you. Managing is keeping things from falling apart. I was mostly doing the second one and calling it the first.

Your question to yourself is a better one than you probably realise. The fact that you're asking it at all is the answer, in a way.

What would *you* change?
records.response_pred:
That's a fair question.

You know the thing that's been bothering me since the rescue got close? It's not the emergency itself or the response to it — it's the amount of time we spent arguing with each other about the right way to do things rather than just doing them. The inventory, the route, the raft, the signal — every single one of those things held up better than I expected but they still held up because we found a way to keep moving rather than get caught in the idea that the perfect plan was more important than the actual plan.

If I'm honest, I've been replaying that over in my head a lot since the rescue got close. I think what I would change — and I say this knowing it's not the kind of thing that's easy to do in the moment — is to spend less of that time thinking about whose fault it is that we're in this situation and more of it thinking about what we actually do next.

The difference between the two is the difference between saying 'this should have been done that way' and saying 'this is what we've got, here's how we use it'. The first gets you stuck. The second gets you out.

It's a small thing, and it's one I'm not pretending I did perfectly even when we were at our best out here. But it's the one thing I think I would genuinely do differently if I had the chance.

The report will be valuable — I'm not saying it won't be. But I think what's actually worth writing down is the route you took to keep people moving through the hard bits. That's the bit that matters.

records.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
records.response_truth:
That sounds like exactly the thing you'd do, and honestly — do it. That data's genuinely valuable and not just for you. If it ends up somewhere useful, if it helps someone else think more clearly about resource management in a survival situation, then something good came out of all of this beyond just the four of us making it home.

But write the last page too. Answer your own question properly, the one you just answered out loud to me — because that's the part that won't show up in the resource data and it's the part that actually matters most. The numbers tell you what happened. That last page tells you *why*.

I'd read that report, for what it's worth. The whole thing, including the last page.
records.response_pred:
Good. You should do that.

You know what I'd suggest you add to the report? The three hours after the crash. How we not fell apart. The things we did to stay with each other when it would've been easy to let go. The order of priorities and why it mattered and how it affected everything else.

That's the actual data. Not the resource tracking, not the decision matrix, not the risk assessment. People. How they behave when it really matters. That's what you should be writing up.

It's not just the right thing to do with the data, either. It's the right thing to do with what just happened. You're not just a survivor, Donatello. You're a participant. And the things you've seen and experienced over the last five days are worth more than any spreadsheet ever could be. You're the one who gets to tell the story of how this group stayed together and what that means for people who come after us.

So yes — do the report. Do it properly. But don't just stop at the resource tracking. Write the real story.

And when you're done, send it to someone who actually needs to read it. Because there's a version of this that needs to be shared with people beyond this campfire.

records.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
records.response_truth:
None. That's the point.

There's no practical purpose to a flower drawn in the sand next to an SOS signal. It doesn't make you more visible from the air, it doesn't conserve water, it doesn't reinforce the keel. By every metric in that notebook it's a complete waste of time.

But DaVinci drew them because he needed to remind himself — and maybe the rest of us — that the reason we were fighting to get seen, to get found, to get *out*, wasn't just biological survival. It was because life has flowers in it. Because there's something worth going back to that isn't just calories and shelter and coordinates.

You asked what practical purpose they served. I'd turn it around. What would it have cost us if he hadn't drawn them? Not in resources — in something harder to measure. Because I watched DaVinci nearly break when that plane passed over us, and I think those flowers were part of what held him together. They were a statement of intent. *We are people, not just survivors. Come and find us.*

That's not nothing, Donatello. That's maybe the most important thing out here. You can keep the lights on with logistics, but you need something like those flowers to make the lights worth keeping on in the first place.

Look at that boat on the horizon and tell me the flowers didn't matter.
records.response_pred:
I think it was just a way to keep his hands moving, to be honest. He needed to keep doing something with them, and drawing was the thing he knew how to do.

But also — and I think this is the thing that's actually more important — they were a reminder that there was beauty in this place before there was anything else. Before there was survival or rescue or any of the rest of it. Just beauty. That's what he was drawing.

People talk about the human spirit and the resilience of the human spirit and all the rest of it, but sometimes what's actually more remarkable is how easily we lose sight of the things that matter when the stakes come up. DaVinci's flowers were a reminder of that, even if he didn't intend them to be. They were a way of saying *this place is not just a survival scenario, it's a place where you can still see something beautiful*.

That's actually really hard to hold onto when you're out here, and I think that's what he was doing. Not just drawing flowers, but holding onto the ability to see them.

records.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
records.response_truth:
Yeah. I'm alright. Just — give me a second.

I don't know what I expected to feel when it happened. Relief, I suppose. Maybe something cleaner than this. But it's strange — I've been so focused on the next thing and the thing after that for three days straight that now there's nothing left to focus on, it's like the whole thing is landing at once and I don't quite know where to put it.

It's a good strange. I just need a moment to let it be real.

You were brilliant out here, you know that? I mean it. Not just the doing — though God knows you did enough of that — but the fact that underneath all the moving and building and keeping everyone going, you were feeling every bit of it. That's not weakness, that's the whole point. That's why the flowers mattered.

Right.

*exhales slowly*

Right. Let's go home.
records.response_pred:
Don't — stop. Just don't stop. You got him to the boat and you got him on the boat and you didn't let him go by himself and I know that's a hard thing to do and I'm saying thank you for it properly now because it's the one thing you haven't actually been thanked for and it matters.

It's not that it's better than the other stuff. It's that it's *different*. It's not the notebook, it's not the food, it's not the route markers. It's something that's going to stay with him for a long time and you're the one who held on to him long enough for him to see it.

He doesn't need to be told it. He just needs to be seen saying it.

You stay there. I need you to see something. *points over DaVinci's shoulder*

That's it. That's the actual thing we've been moving toward for five days, the thing we've been doing everything to reach. The person who was standing on the edge of the water earlier, the person who was crying, the person who drew flowers in the sand — that's the person who just said what he said to you.

That's the actual data point, Donatello. The one that tells you everything matters, not just the logistics or the decisions or even the person who's making them. *starts walking toward the water*

You go back there. I'll stay and talk to him for the next five minutes. What he needs right now is for someone to say something back to him, and I'm not the person who can do that for him.

You go back there and say it. Say it to yourself, say it to him, say it to the water, say it to the air — *whatever* that makes the words real to you. Because I'm saying it to you, and I know you need to hear it from someone.

You are seen. You are heard. You are valued. You are not disposable. You are not alone.

*stops walking and turns back*

And when you come back, we're going to eat something together. Properly. Because we're done being hungry, and we're done being scared, and we're done being alone.

records.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
records.response_truth:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on then — stay close, same as you have done since the start.

You know, when we landed I thought you were the one I'd have to carry through this. Turns out you were paying attention to everything the whole time, flagging things no one else was catching, asking the questions the rest of us were too busy to stop and ask. That's not nothing. That's actually quite a lot.

So yeah. We go together. Same as everything else out here.

After you.
records.response_pred:
No. You go first. I care more about you getting out of here safely than I do about being the one to cross that line.

Donatello — your family are there. Go to your family. I'll be right behind you.

And when you're clear of it — when you're actually clear of it and back in the real world and able to breathe properly again — don't let the clarity of perspective that happens after survival make you forget what you did out here. Don't let it make you forget the people who held together rather than just being held, the people who made the actual difference.

You're the one with the notebook and the data and the analysis. You're the one who's going to write the report that tells people what to do better next time.

But you're also the one who drew flowers in the sand and told people they were worth fighting for.

Don't lose that.
